Arapaho

Arapaho people, identified as Hinono’ei in the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes’ account, maintain distinct northern and southern political communities. Their history includes wide-ranging Plains homelands, alliance with Cheyenne people, violent dispossession and continuing language and cultural work. Northern Arapaho institutions at Wind River and the Oklahoma government require separate attention.

An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
01

Homelands and northern and southern communities

The Arapaho Project describes historical lands extending across the central Plains and toward the Rocky Mountains, rather than a homeland confined to one modern state. In the nineteenth century, northern and southern groups centered increasingly on the North Platte and Arkansas river valleys. Bison hunting, horses and trade were central to life on the Plains. The history emphasizes alliance with Cheyenne people. Northern Arapaho settled at Wind River in 1878; Southern Arapaho histories led to west-central Oklahoma, producing different reservation and governmental experiences.

Read the sources [5] The Arapaho Project / University of Colorado Boulder

02

Sand Creek and the consequences of dispossession

On November 29, 1864, Colorado volunteer soldiers attacked a Cheyenne and Arapaho encampment at Sand Creek. The National Park Service identifies many of the victims as women, children and elderly people. This massacre forms part of the violent process through which settlers and governments displaced communities from their lands. Its history also survives through families. Descendants and tribal leaders undertook oral-history investigations that helped identify the massacre site, alongside documentary and archaeological work. The national historic site opened in 2007 after that collaborative research.

Read the sources [7] National Park Service

03

Separate governments and contemporary public services

The Northern Arapaho Tribe’s official site places it on the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming and provides access to its Business Council and tribal codes. Its department directory includes family services, water and sewer operations, vocational rehabilitation and immersion education. The Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes government in Oklahoma presents executive, legislative, judicial and Tribal Council branches; the Tribal Council includes adult tribal members. These public institutions show why references to an Arapaho cultural community must be distinguished from the powers and organization of a particular sovereign government.

Read the sources [2] Northern Arapaho Tribe [3] Northern Arapaho Tribe [4] Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes

04

Language learning across generations

Arapaho belongs to the Algonquian language family, with a distinctive history of sound change that makes it differ considerably from many relatives. The Arapaho Project links grammar, pronunciation, stories, lessons and dictionaries for learners. The Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes describe community and online classes, youth language outreach, Elder participation and an adult Master Apprentice program. Northern Arapaho’s directory separately lists immersion education at Ethete. These initiatives involve teaching and relationships among generations, extending beyond the preservation of recordings or written materials alone.

Read the sources [1] Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes [3] Northern Arapaho Tribe [6] The Arapaho Project / University of Colorado Boulder

05

Cultural authority, repatriation and historical interpretation

The Cheyenne and Arapaho Culture Program includes representatives working on the return of ancestral remains and funerary belongings from institutions. It also includes Sand Creek representatives who work with the National Park Service on how the massacre is presented publicly. Together with descendants’ role in identifying the site, this demonstrates that communities participate in deciding how history is researched, cared for and explained. Their cultural work connects living families, ancestral places, language teaching and obligations toward earlier generations, rather than treating heritage as a collection of detached museum objects.

Read the sources [1] Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes [7] National Park Service
